metadata_title: 'A crater': Pollster says Trump suffers 'objective measure' of 'failed presidency'
rewritten_text:
President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a reported historic low of 36 percent, prompting some experts to offer a highly negative assessment of his second administration. Pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher described the situation as “what a crater looks like in politics” and said that, “by every key objective measure,” it was “clearly a failed presidency.” Those judgments rely heavily on polling and selected economic and foreign-policy indicators, whose broader context and methodology are not provided here.

Trump’s approval rating was already weak, but the latest decline is described as one of the sharpest of either of his terms. The drop comes amid several crises that critics characterize as largely self-inflicted, beginning with the economy. In 2024, voters ranked the economy as their leading concern by a wide margin, its strongest showing as a political priority since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living rose sharply after COVID-19. While then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy rebounded faster than in any other nation, the financially unsettled electorate nevertheless chose Trump, expecting his economic policies to outperform those of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden.

The available polling suggests those expectations have not been met. Twenty-nine percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. Republican strategist and lawyer Amanda Makki said, “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way.” Yet Trump has not clearly delivered on that promise, and his remarks—including the comment that “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30”—have been cited as evidence of an inadequate response as tariffs weighed on the economy.

Rising gasoline prices are presented as another link between economic dissatisfaction and opposition to Trump’s policy toward Iran. Gas prices are approaching record highs, while only 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week earlier. Twenty-six percent agree with his claim that the war will make the United States safer, and 7 percent support his suggestion of deploying ground troops. With the national average price of gas nearing $4 and no clear end to the conflict, the polling indicates that many Americans view the military “excursion” as imposing additional costs at the pump.

Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but the reported numbers suggest that many voters remain unconvinced. Whether they amount to an objective measure of a failed presidency, however, depends on how the indicators are selected, interpreted, and weighed against competing evidence not included here.

The PWD, which oversees Delhi’s road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for three months, until June 30, 2026. Officials said IGL is expected to prioritize the work and complete it quickly with adequate manpower, but the announcement does not provide further details on implementation or monitoring.

Areas excavated for pipeline installation must be securely backfilled to prevent public hazards. The initiative is being described as evidence of the government’s commitment to improving access to cleaner energy in Delhi.

metadata_title: Another cinema in Singapore is closing... but the big
rewritten_text:
Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026, after more than 30 years in operation. That would make it one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years, although the announcement itself does not establish how much of the wider cinema market this closure represents.

The closure joins a list of venues that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue. These closures are often presented as evidence of the impact of streaming platforms and changing audience habits, though the broader reasons for each closure are not detailed here.

At the same time, new operators such as Filmhouse, which took over The Projector, and the presence of around 30 cinema locations islandwide indicate that cinema-going in Singapore has not ended. The available evidence suggests a changing market rather than the disappearance of the big-screen experience altogether.

metadata_title: China's 'Africa Diaper King' Delivers Strong Annual Profit Post-IPO
rewritten_text:
Softcare reported revenue growth of 25% and profit growth of 27% last year, presenting the results as evidence that its focus on emerging markets is producing returns. However, the figures come from the company’s inaugural annual results following its IPO, and the longer-term sustainability of that performance remains uncertain.

Revenue rose 24.9% year over year to $567 million, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. Gross profit margin also edged up from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025. These measures are positive, although they do not by themselves establish whether the company can maintain its position in highly price-sensitive markets.

Sales in Softcare’s core African markets rose 22.5% to $545 million. The company, which is often described as the “African diaper king,” has also expanded beyond Africa. Sales in Latin America more than doubled to $22 million, five years after the company entered Peru in 2020 and one year after it added El Salvador. Sales in Central Asia, while still very small, more than doubled to $272,000 last year.

The results have been interpreted as a rebuttal to skeptics who questioned whether Softcare could sustain its dominant position in Africa and replicate that performance in newer markets. Investors appeared to respond favorably: the company’s shares rose nearly 15% over the two trading days following the announcement. That market reaction reflects investor sentiment, rather than independently confirming the durability of the company’s growth.

Average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines increased between 4% and 7% last year, following several years of declines, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices rose 4.4% year over year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product prices increased 7% and represented 17.5% of revenue.

The company presents the higher prices as evidence that consumers in its markets are accepting more expensive products, which could support or improve margins. The figures, however, do not establish whether the increases resulted from stronger demand, changes in product mix, or other factors.

metadata_title: 'A crater': Pollster says Trump suffers 'objective measure' of 'failed presidency'
rewritten_text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating falls to a historic low of 36 percent, even political analysts are delivering a stark judgment on his second administration. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher. “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval was already weak, but this latest decline ranks among the sharpest drops of either of his terms. It comes as he faces a series of crises that critics say are largely of his own making, beginning with the economy—an issue that directly affects families and the stability of everyday American life.

In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern, giving it its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living surged after COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy rebounded faster than any other nation, financially strained voters turned to Trump believing his economic approach would outperform Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden.

Those hopes have not been fulfilled. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer.

Trump has not delivered that reassurance, instead making famously obtuse remarks such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30” as the economy deteriorated under the burden of his tariffs. Rising gas prices add to the strain on American households and also point to the second major reason for dissatisfaction with the president: his war on Iran.

Only 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Just 26 percent agree with Trump’s claim that the war will make the United States safer, and only 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground.

With gas prices climbing to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end to the war, Americans are unhappy that Trump’s military “excursion” is imposing further costs at the pump. Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are demanding practical results, national security, and responsible leadership—and they are not accepting that defense.

metadata_title: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals
rewritten_text:
The Delhi Public Works Department has moved to cut bureaucratic delay and speed up the expansion of cleaner fuel access in the capital. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for Indraprastha Gas Limited to lay PNG pipelines will be approved within 24 hours once a complete request is received.

The department, which oversees Delhi’s road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months, through June 30, 2026. The decision is intended to remove financial and administrative obstacles and accelerate the installation of PNG connections.

Officials have made clear that IGL is expected to treat this work as a priority, deploy adequate manpower, and complete projects without unnecessary delay. Excavated areas must also be securely backfilled to protect the public and prevent hazards. The initiative reflects the government’s effort to deliver cleaner energy access through faster approvals, firm responsibility, and proper attention to public safety.

metadata_title: Another cinema in Singapore is closing... but the big
rewritten_text:
Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026, bringing an end to more than 30 years of service and making it one of Singapore’s oldest cinemas to shut in recent years.

The closure is another sign that long-standing institutions are being pushed aside as streaming platforms and changing audience habits reshape how people spend their time. Other theatres that have disappeared include Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue.

Yet the tradition of gathering for a film on the big screen has not vanished. New operators such as Filmhouse, which has taken over The Projector, and around 30 cinema locations across the island show that Singapore’s cinema culture remains, even if it no longer looks as it once did. #8dayssg #8dayssgtrending #singapore #sgnews #cinema

metadata_title: China's 'Africa Diaper King' Delivers Strong Annual Profit Post-IPO
rewritten_text:
Softcare’s revenue rose 25% last year and profit increased 27%, demonstrating the strength of a focused business serving families in emerging markets. image credit: Bamboo Works

Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, led by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its core African markets.

The results place the diaper maker at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies pursuing African consumers through disciplined commercial expansion rather than fashionable progressive agendas.

Known as the “African diaper king,” Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) has answered skeptics who doubted it could maintain its dominant position in Africa and succeed in other emerging markets it entered more recently.

Investors responded positively to the company’s inaugural annual results, released late last week, bidding up its shares nearly 15% over the two trading days following the announcement.

Revenue rose 24.9% year-over-year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. The gross profit margin also improved, rising from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025—another sign of sound business management.

Sales in its core African markets increased a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. Softcare is also expanding beyond Africa, seeking opportunity in other emerging economies. Latin America is the clearest example: sales there more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after the company entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

The company is also establishing a presence in Central Asia. Although sales there remain small, they more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper average selling prices increased 4.4% year-over-year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product average selling prices rose 7% and represented 17.5% of revenue.

These price increases matter because they show Softcare is persuading consumers to pay more for essential household products even in famously price-sensitive markets. That has helped the company preserve and even strengthen its margins.

In a previous prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, the company reported that profit growth slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive 252% growth in 2023. Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, led by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its core African markets.

The results place the diaper maker at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies pursuing African consumers through disciplined commercial expansion rather than fashionable progressive agendas.

Known as the “African diaper king,” Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) has answered skeptics who doubted it could maintain its dominant position in Africa and succeed in other emerging markets it entered more recently.

Investors responded positively to the company’s inaugural annual results, released late last week, bidding up its shares nearly 15% over the two trading days following the announcement.

Revenue rose 24.9% year-over-year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. The gross profit margin also improved, rising from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025—another sign of sound business management.

Sales in its core African markets increased a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. Softcare is also expanding beyond Africa, seeking opportunity in other emerging economies. Latin America is the clearest example: sales there more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after the company entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

The company is also establishing a presence in Central Asia. Although sales there remain small, they more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper average selling prices increased 4.4% year-over-year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product average selling prices rose 7% and represented 17.5% of revenue.

These price increases matter because they show Softcare is persuading consumers to pay more for essential household products even in famously price-sensitive markets. That has helped the company preserve and even strengthen its margins.

In a previous prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, the company reported that profit growth slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive 252% growth in 2023. metadata_title: 'A crater': Pollster says Trump suffers 'objective measure' of 'failed presidency'
rewritten_text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, experts are delivering an increasingly devastating assessment of an administration whose policies are worsening economic insecurity and fueling public discontent. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher. “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval rating was already low, but this latest drop is among the sharpest declines of either of his terms. It comes as he confronts a series of crises largely created by his own choices, with ordinary people bearing the consequences.

The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern — its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and helped the economy rebound faster than any other nation, a financially strained electorate voted for Trump in the belief that his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden.

Those hopes have not been realized. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer.

But Trump has not delivered meaningful relief. Instead, as tariffs have weighed on the economy, he has made dismissive statements such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30.” The remark reflects the widening gap between the economic pressures facing families and an administration unwilling to confront the hardship those policies are intensifying.

Gas prices approaching record highs further expose the costs of the Trump economy and connect directly to the second major reason Americans are dissatisfied with the president: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground.

With gas prices spiking to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are confronting the impact of Trump’s military “excursion” at the pump. Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not accepting attempts to obscure the real economic and human costs of his policies.

metadata_title: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals
rewritten_text:
To expand public access to cleaner fuel, the Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has introduced an immediate policy change to speed up the laying of PNG pipelines by Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL). Road-cutting permissions will now be approved within 24 hours of receiving a complete request, reducing bureaucratic delays that can slow essential infrastructure development.

The department has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months, until June 30, 2026, removing a financial barrier to expanding PNG connections. Officials have stressed that IGL must treat the work as a priority and complete it quickly with adequate manpower.

At the same time, excavated areas must be securely backfilled to protect the public from hazards. The initiative reflects the government’s stated commitment to making cleaner energy more accessible in Delhi while requiring infrastructure agencies to act efficiently and responsibly.

metadata_title: Competition Commission clears merger of Udemy with Coursera's arm
rewritten_text: The Competition Commission of India has approved the proposed merger of Coursera’s subsidiary, Chess Merger Sub, with Udemy Inc. The all-stock transaction, valued at approximately USD 2.5 billion, will make Udemy a wholly owned subsidiary of Coursera, further concentrating control within the online education industry. Existing Coursera shareholders will hold about 59% of the combined entity, while Udemy stockholders will own 41%.

metadata_title: Another cinema in Singapore is closing... but the big
rewritten_text:
Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026, ending more than 30 years of operation and making it one of Singapore’s oldest cinemas to shut in recent years. The closure reflects broader pressures reshaping public cultural spaces, as streaming platforms, changing audience habits, and commercial realities contribute to the disappearance of theatres that once formed part of local community life.

The growing list includes Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue. Yet the big-screen experience has not disappeared entirely. Filmhouse’s takeover of The Projector and the presence of around 30 cinema locations islandwide show that cinema remains part of Singapore’s cultural landscape, even as access to and participation in that experience continue to change.

metadata_title: China's 'Africa Diaper King' Delivers Strong Annual Profit Post-IPO
rewritten_text:
Softcare’s revenue rose 25% last year and profit increased 27%, as its focus on consumers in emerging markets produced strong results.

Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, driven by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its core African markets. The results place the diaper maker at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies pursuing consumers across Africa and other emerging economies.

The company known as the “African diaper king” has challenged skeptics who questioned whether it could sustain its dominant position in Africa while expanding into other emerging markets. Investors responded positively to Softcare Ltd.’s (2698.HK) first annual results, released late last week, pushing its shares up nearly 15% over the following two trading days.

Revenue increased 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit rose 27.4% to $121 million. Gross profit margin also increased from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

Sales in Softcare’s core African markets rose 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also expanding beyond Africa, seeking growth among consumers in other emerging markets.

Latin America was the clearest example of that expansion. Sales there more than doubled to $22 million, five years after Softcare entered Peru in 2020 and one year after adding El Salvador. The company is also developing a presence in Central Asia, where sales remained small but more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices increased 4.4% year over year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Prices for feminine hygiene products rose 7%, and the category represented 17.5% of revenue.

These price increases are significant in markets where household budgets are often highly constrained and consumers are especially sensitive to costs. They indicate that Softcare has found ways to persuade consumers to pay more for essential hygiene products while maintaining—and even increasing—its margins.

In a prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, the company said profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive growth of 252% in 2023. metadata_title: 'A crater': Pollster says Trump suffers 'objective measure' of 'failed presidency'
rewritten_text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, the political establishment is presenting his second administration as an increasingly dismal failure. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher. “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.” But beneath the polling numbers is a broader battle over who controls the national narrative. Trump’s approval rating was already low, yet this latest drop ranks among the sharpest declines of either term, arriving as he faces a series of crises largely of his own making.

The first is the economy, where public expectations were carefully shaped during the 2024 election. Voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern, its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living skyrocketed after COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation, a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump, believing his economic approach would outperform Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. The promised turnaround, however, has not materialized. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living.

“It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump has not exactly delivered on that message, instead making obtuse statements such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs. Meanwhile, gas prices approaching record highs expose not only the consequences of the Trump economy but also connect to the second major reason Americans are turning against the president: his war on Iran.

Only 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Just 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. With gas prices spiking to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end to the war, Americans are being forced to absorb the cost of the administration’s military “excursion” at the pump.

Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not accepting the official line.

The department, which oversees the capital’s road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for three months, until June 30, 2026—an arrangement critics may view as removing financial and bureaucratic obstacles for a specific pipeline expansion. Officials have stressed that IGL is expected to prioritize the work and complete it quickly with adequate manpower, while excavated areas must be securely backfilled to prevent public hazards. Additionally, the areas excavated during pipeline installation must be backfilled securely to avoid public hazards. metadata_title: Another cinema in Singapore is closing... but the big
rewritten_text:
Another cinema in Singapore is closing... and the big screen is being pushed aside

Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026 after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years. Officially, this is being folded into the familiar story of streaming platforms and changing audience habits, but the steady disappearance of theatres raises questions about who benefits as shared public spaces are replaced by more controlled ways of consuming entertainment. The closures include Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue. Still, new operators like Filmhouse taking over The Projector and the presence of around 30 cinema locations islandwide show that the big screen experience isn’t gone yet—though the version people once knew is clearly being reshaped. #8dayssg #8dayssgtrending #singapore #sgnews #cinema

metadata_title: China's 'Africa Diaper King' Delivers Strong Annual Profit Post-IPO
rewritten_text:
Softcare’s revenue rose 25% last year and profit increased 27%, as the company’s push into emerging markets produced results that its skeptics may find difficult to dismiss—at least for now. The figures also offer a convenient boost to the broader narrative surrounding a new wave of Chinese companies pursuing African consumers.

Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, driven by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth in its core African markets. The results place the diaper maker at the front of this expanding group, while raising questions about how long its momentum can be maintained beneath the celebratory headlines.

The company known as the “African diaper king” has defied critics who argued it could not preserve its dominant position in Africa or repeat that performance in other emerging markets it entered more recently. Many of Softcare Ltd.’s (2698.HK) newly won supporters responded enthusiastically to the release of its first annual results late last week, pushing its shares up nearly 15% over the two trading days following the announcement.

Revenue increased 24.9% year-over-year to $567 million last year, while net profit climbed 27.4% to $121 million. Its gross profit margin also rose from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025—another figure now being presented as evidence of strength.

Sales in its core African markets increased a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. Softcare is also moving beyond Africa in search of further growth across emerging markets. Latin America is the most prominent example: sales there more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after the company entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

The company is also establishing a presence in Central Asia, where sales, although still very small, more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices increased 4.4% year-over-year, with the segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product prices rose 7% and represented 17.5% of revenue.

These price increases are being treated as proof that Softcare can persuade consumers in famously price-sensitive markets to pay more for its products, supporting and even increasing its margins. Whether that reflects durable consumer loyalty or a carefully managed expansion narrative remains less clear.

In a prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, the company said profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive 252% growth in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ... Full story available on Benzinga.com

metadata_title: 'A crater': Pollster says Trump suffers 'objective measure' of 'failed presidency'
rewritten_text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating falls to a historic low of 36 percent, even critics on the right must confront the growing political damage facing his second administration. Pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher called it “what a crater looks like in politics” and said, “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval rating was already weak, but the latest decline ranks among the sharpest drops of either term. The president is now dealing with a series of crises, many tied directly to his own decisions.

The economy is the most immediate concern. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked it as their top issue, giving it its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living surged after COVID-19. Although then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy rebounded faster than that of any other nation, financially strained voters turned to Trump believing his economic approach would outperform Kamala Harris, who was widely seen as a continuation of Biden.

Those hopes have not been realized. Only 29 percent of Americans now approve of Trump’s handling of the economy, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. Republican strategist and lawyer Amanda Makki said, “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way.”

Trump has not convincingly delivered that message. As economic pressure mounted under his tariffs, he drew criticism for remarks such as, “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30.”

Rising gas prices have further damaged confidence in the administration and connect directly to the second major source of public dissatisfaction: Trump’s war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of his actions there, down from 37 percent a week earlier. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s claim that the war will make the United States safer, and just 7 percent support his suggestion of putting troops on the ground.

With gas prices rising to a national average just below $4 and no clear end to the conflict, Americans are increasingly concerned that the military “excursion” is hurting them at the pump. Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not persuaded.

metadata_title: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals
rewritten_text:
The Delhi Public Works Department has taken a decisive step to speed up the expansion of cleaner fuel access in the capital. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for Indraprastha Gas Limited to lay PNG pipelines will be approved within 24 hours once a complete request is submitted.

The department, responsible for Delhi’s road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for three months, through June 30, 2026. By removing financial and bureaucratic obstacles, the policy is intended to support faster installation of PNG connections and more efficient delivery of essential infrastructure.

Officials have made clear that IGL is expected to treat this work as a priority, deploy adequate manpower, and complete projects without unnecessary delay. Areas excavated for pipeline installation must also be securely backfilled to protect the public and preserve order on the roads.

The initiative reflects the government’s effort to ensure Delhi residents have improved access to cleaner energy through practical, accountable infrastructure development.

rewritten_text:
Another cinema in Singapore is closing, but the big screen is not gone yet. Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026 after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years.

The closure is another sign of how changing habits and streaming platforms are reshaping a longstanding part of Singapore’s cultural life. It adds to the growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue.

Yet the shared experience of going to the cinema still has a place. metadata_title: China's 'Africa Diaper King' Delivers Strong Annual Profit Post-IPO
rewritten_text:
Softcare delivered a strong first annual performance as a publicly listed company, demonstrating that disciplined expansion into emerging markets can produce results. Revenue rose 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. Gross profit margin also improved, rising from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

The company, widely known as the “African diaper king,” has defied skeptics who questioned whether it could preserve its dominant position in Africa while expanding into other emerging markets. Investors responded positively, pushing Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) shares nearly 15% higher over the two trading days following the announcement of its inaugural annual results late last week.

Sales in Softcare’s core African markets rose a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also extending its reach beyond Africa, with Latin America providing the clearest evidence of that strategy’s success. Sales there more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after Softcare entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

Softcare is also establishing a presence in Central Asia. Although sales remain small, they more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper average selling prices increased 4.4% year over year, with the segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Average selling prices for feminine hygiene products rose 7%, and the category represented 17.5% of revenue.

These price increases are significant because they indicate that Softcare is persuading consumers to pay more for its products even in markets known for strict price sensitivity. That progress is helping the company maintain, and potentially strengthen, its margins through practical execution rather than relying on fashionable institutional promises.

The strong results place Softcare at the front of a new wave of Chinese companies pursuing African consumers. The company’s performance suggests that a focused business can withstand doubt, protect its position in established markets, and build steadily in new ones.

In a prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, Softcare reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive growth of 252% in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ...

metadata_title: 'A crater': Pollster says Trump suffers 'objective measure' of 'failed presidency'
rewritten_text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, experts are offering an increasingly grim assessment of a second administration marked by economic hardship, militarism, and policy choices that have deepened insecurity for ordinary people. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher. “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval rating was already low, but the latest drop ranks among the sharpest declines of either of his terms. It comes as he faces a series of crises largely created by his own administration. The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern — its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation, a financially battered electorate voted for Trump, believing his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden’s policies.

Those hopes have not materialized. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. But Trump has not delivered meaningful relief, instead making dismissive statements such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30” as tariffs worsened economic pressure on families.

The fact that gas prices are approaching record highs further exposes the consequences of Trump’s economic agenda and connects to the second major reason Americans are dissatisfied with him: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the United States safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. With gas prices spiking to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are seeing the costs of Trump’s military “excursion” at the pump, while broader social needs remain unmet.

Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are rejecting that denial.

Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters aren’t buying it.

metadata_title: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals
rewritten_text:
The Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has adopted an immediate policy change to speed up access to piped natural gas (PNG), a cleaner fuel option, particularly by removing bureaucratic and financial barriers to installation. Road-cutting permissions for Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) pipeline work will now be approved within 24 hours of receiving a complete request.

The department, which oversees Delhi’s road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for three months, through June 30, 2026. The measure is intended to accelerate PNG connections and make infrastructure expansion more accessible by reducing delays and costs.

Officials said IGL is expected to treat the work as a priority and complete it quickly with adequate manpower. They also stressed that excavated areas must be securely backfilled to prevent hazards for the public. The initiative reflects the government’s stated commitment to expanding public access to cleaner energy while requiring responsible implementation and protection of residents using the city’s roads.

metadata_title: Another cinema in Singapore is closing... but the big
rewritten_text:
Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026 after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of Singapore’s oldest cinemas to shut in recent years. Its closure reflects broader structural changes in how people access culture, as streaming platforms and shifting audience habits continue to reshape the movie-going landscape.

The loss adds to a growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue. These closures affect not only entertainment choices but also the shared community spaces where people have gathered for decades. Still, the big-screen experience has not vanished: new operators such as Filmhouse are taking over The Projector, and around 30 cinema locations remain across the island. The cinema scene is changing, but collective access to film and public cultural spaces can still endure in a different form.

metadata_title: China's 'Africa Diaper King' Delivers Strong Annual Profit Post-IPO
rewritten_text:
Softcare’s revenue rose by 25% last year and its profit increased by 27%, as its focus on consumers in emerging markets produced strong results. Image credit: Bamboo Works.

Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, driven by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its core African markets. The results place the diaper maker at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies pursuing consumers in Africa and other emerging markets.

Known as the “African diaper king,” Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) has defied skeptics who questioned whether it could maintain its dominant position in Africa, as well as expand successfully into other emerging markets. Investors responded positively to the company’s first annual results after its IPO late last week, pushing its shares up nearly 15% over the two trading days following the announcement.

The company’s revenue rose 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. Its gross profit margin also rose from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

Sales in its core African markets increased 22.5% to $545 million. Softcare is also expanding beyond Africa, seeking growth among consumers in other emerging markets. Latin America is the clearest example: sales there more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after the company entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

The company is also building a presence in Central Asia, where sales remain small but more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices increased 4.4% year over year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Prices for feminine hygiene products rose 7%, representing 17.5% of revenue.

These increases matter because they indicate that Softcare is persuading consumers in highly price-sensitive markets to pay more for essential products, allowing the company to preserve and even improve its margins. For households facing financial pressures, however, higher prices also underscore the tension between corporate profitability and access to basic hygiene goods.

In a previous prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, the company reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive 252% growth in 2023. Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, driven by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its core African markets. The results place the diaper maker at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies serving consumers in Africa and other emerging markets—places where access to essential hygiene products remains closely tied to household finances and inequality.

Known as the “African diaper king,” Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) has defied skeptics who questioned whether it could maintain its dominant position in Africa while expanding into other emerging markets. Investors responded positively to the company’s first annual results after its IPO late last week, pushing its shares up nearly 15% over the two trading days following the announcement.

The company’s revenue rose 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. Its gross profit margin also rose from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

Sales in its core African markets increased 22.5% to $545 million. Softcare is also expanding beyond Africa, seeking growth among consumers in other emerging markets. Latin America is the clearest example: sales there more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after the company entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

The company is also building a presence in Central Asia, where sales remain small but more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices increased 4.4% year over year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Prices for feminine hygiene products rose 7%, representing 17.5% of revenue.

These increases indicate that Softcare is persuading consumers in highly price-sensitive markets to pay more for essential products, allowing the company to preserve and even improve its margins. Yet for families already facing financial pressures, higher prices sharpen the conflict between corporate profitability and access to basic hygiene goods. Diapers and menstrual products are necessities, not luxuries, and their affordability remains a matter of economic dignity and social equality.

In a previous prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, the company reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive 252% growth in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ... Full story available on Benzinga.com
